newsitem.title: UK: Derivatives can help banks' credit status - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives can help banks' credit status - Moody's.

text.p: Financial institutions could improve their creditworthiness through the use of credit risk management based on statistics, and hedging with credit derivatives, according to a report by Moody's Investors Service.
However, while European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is likely to accelerate use of these instruments, there will still be a place for sound lending judgement, the agency said.
"These new developments, however far-reaching, will not simply transform banks into risk-free organisations," it said.
Among the benefits are more active management of most loan-portfolio segments, more accurate loan-loss provisioning, and risk-adjusted loan pricing, the credit agency said.
"Banking in general, and lending money in particular, will remain very much a people's business, rather than a model-driven decision," it added.

Moody's said many institutions were reluctant to adopt loan pricing methodologies based on so-called "risk-adjusted return on capital", or RAROC. There were also concerns about the compatibility of risk management models with loan portfolios.

The agency said links between local economic cycles may not be adequately demonstrated by universally applicable matrices, and the differing behaviour of business cycles in markets means there could also be differences in loan-repayment behaviour.
For example, repayment delays could be more acceptable in countries with less developed domestic capital markets where market discipline is less solidly entrenched.

However, Moody's said that if EMU becomes a reality, the creation and development of a viable secondary bank-loan market in Europe is possible -- and that would in turn strengthen the discipline and predictability of loan-repayment behaviour.

It said in an ideal world, banks would base their lending on default-predictability models, build actuarial provisions incrementally according to these models, and charge borrowers based on RAROC pricing to incorporate the credit-risk element.
Moody's said this ideal scenario was far off, and banks were unlikely to be able to immunise their lending risk completely for the foreseeable future.

But modern risk management and the use of credit derivatives should usher in a new lending culture, which is increasingly concerned with risk-adjusted earnings and with efficient capital management, rather than a way to boost assets and market shares.

"The broader shift in banks' intellectual universe toward positioning themselves on an efficient frontier of risks and returns, away from the old asset-growth strategies, may in fact be the main gain from these new developments," the report said.
